newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY MOL UNAWARE OF PLANS TO ALTER SALE TERMS.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY MOL UNAWARE OF PLANS TO ALTER SALE TERMS.

text.p: An official at Hungarian oil and gas company MOL said on Tuesday he was unaware of plans to alter the conditions for the sale of state-owned shares in the company following press reports of an offer from the U.S. company Tenneco to buy MOL's gas division.
According to Tuesday's Hungarian daily Magyar Hirlap the state privatisation agency APV rejected the offer without consulting MOL as it was against breaking up the company.
It also reportedly decided on a public issue of a total 33 percent of shares in two phases at the beginning and end of this year.

"We were not in contact with Tenneco and we have not received any offer with regard to buying any shares in any of our businesses," Zoltan Aldott, MOL's director for international markets told Reuters on Tuesday.
Tenneco's offer to buy the gas division reportedly involved seeking a majority stake by buying a large number of MOL shares on the stock exchange as well as acquiring the 33 percent stake from APV.
Under the terms of the law allowing the privatisation of MOL, foreign oil firms are prevented from gaining a majority stake in order to maintain MOL as the "national oil company".
However, Hungary's ministry of industry and trade is reported to favour modifying the law in order to hive off the gas sector for separate sale.
Aldott said such a move would involve a number of technical difficulties, including the fact that Hungary's oil and gas fields are located in the same area.

"MOL is responsible for the operation of the whole of Hungarian high pressure system and that comes partly from fields which are located in Hungary and which in many cases are jointly oil and gas fields," he said.
"There are also gas storages amd imports, and all three (gas activities) should be coordinated quite closely."
However, Aldott added the ultimate decision was economic.

"I don't think it's a technical matter, it's a business matter and I'd like to underline that as in the case of many other large international oil and gas companies, gas is a good prospect and a growing business."
MOL is Hungary's exclusive supplier of gas and recent wholesale price rises of an average 16.9 percent are seen by annalysts as ensuring a healthy profit for the company.

Regarding the timing of the share issue Gabor Racz, APV's head of energy privatisations, was quoted by Magyar Hirlap as saying the 33 percent stake with a total face value of 32 billion forints would be offered to domestic and international investors in the first and fourth quarters of the year.
Racz told Reuters he was not authorised to comment further on the report but Aldott said delaying the issue of some of the shares could make sense depending on future price trends.

"There should be flexibility," he said. "If there is good demand and the price is right it might be good for the government to sell a larger chunk ahead but if they believe the price will improve it makes sense to spread the sale over a longer time period," he said.
The sale conditions also stipulate that the state should retain permenently a stake of 25 percent plus one golden share, ensuring special voting rights.
